initial_requirements: Ejada needs a supply chain management system to coordinate delivery of its information-technology products, consulting, and related services. Staff should be able to manage customer service, procurement, supplier and material selection, product development, manufacturing flow, physical distribution, outsourcing, and partnerships. The system should also help the company assess cost, productivity, assets, service, and quality performance across the supply chain.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What are the primary business outcomes and success criteria you want this supply chain management system to achieve for Ejada?
turns.interviewee_utterance: The main outcome we want is better end-to-end visibility and control across procurement, delivery, and service execution so we can respond faster and reduce delays. We also want clearer cost management, stronger supplier performance, and better coordination between teams so our projects and customer commitments are met more reliably. Success would mean fewer stock or delivery issues, improved productivity, more accurate planning, and better service quality that we can measure across the supply chain.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Which stakeholder roles will use or be affected by the system, and what responsibilities or decisions should each role have across procurement, delivery, service execution, and performance monitoring?
turns.interviewee_utterance: The main users will be procurement staff, supply chain managers, warehouse or logistics staff, project or service delivery teams, finance or operations management, and probably supplier partners in some limited way. Procurement staff would handle supplier selection, purchase requests, and order follow-up, while delivery and warehouse teams would manage receiving, dispatching, and tracking materials. Service delivery teams would use it to coordinate product or service execution, and managers would review performance, costs, delays, and quality so they can approve decisions and intervene when needed.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Are there any exception cases, operational boundaries, or external systems that the supply chain management system must handle or integrate with—for example, specific failure scenarios, escalation rules, handoffs, or existing ERP, procurement, inventory, finance, or logistics platforms?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, there will definitely be exceptions and handoffs, especially when supplier deliveries are late, items arrive damaged, approvals are delayed, or a service commitment changes at the last minute. In those cases, the system should support escalation to a manager or the relevant team so action can be taken quickly, but the exact thresholds and rules still need to be confirmed with operations. We also expect it to integrate with whatever ERP, finance, and inventory tools we already use, plus possibly logistics or tracking platforms, but I’d need to verify which systems are currently in place.

turns.interviewer_utterance: For the exception cases you mentioned—late deliveries, damaged items, delayed approvals, and last-minute service changes—what specific thresholds, timing rules, or conditions should trigger escalation, and who should each type of escalation go to?
turns.interviewee_utterance: For late deliveries, I’d expect escalation if a supplier misses the committed date or if there’s no confirmed update within a defined grace period, but the exact number of hours or days hasn’t been agreed yet. Damaged items should probably escalate immediately to procurement and warehouse or receiving, with finance or the supplier contacted if replacement or credit is needed. Delayed approvals should go to the approver’s manager after a set time limit, and last-minute service changes should escalate to the delivery or operations lead so they can reassign work and notify the customer if needed.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Could you describe the manufacturing and production workflows the system needs to support, including the main steps, handoffs, approvals, and any differences between work done internally versus work that is outsourced?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Internally, the workflow should cover planning the work, checking material availability, releasing the job to production, tracking progress, and then recording completion and quality checks before handoff. There are usually approvals at the point of releasing a job and again if materials, scope, or schedule change. For outsourced work, the system should track the same order or service request, but with handoff to the external partner, milestone tracking, and acceptance when the partner delivers back to us; the main difference is that we need tighter visibility on supplier progress rather than direct shop-floor control.

turns.interviewer_utterance: When a new product or service is being introduced, what stage-gates or approval checkpoints should the system enforce from idea or request through to launch, and what criteria or approvals are required at each gate?
turns.interviewee_utterance: We’d want the system to support a few clear checkpoints, starting with an initial request or concept review to make sure the idea is valid and aligned with business need. Then there should be a feasibility and cost review, where product, operations, procurement, and finance confirm we can deliver it and that the margins or budgets make sense. After that, there should be a readiness approval before launch, covering materials, supplier capacity, service resources, and any quality or compliance checks, but the exact approvers and criteria may vary depending on the product or service.
